doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: What makes black music black: Duke Ellington and Booker T and the MGs
summary: Asked what makes black music, he quotes Duke Ellington and cites the white Muscle Shoals rhythm section and Booker T and the MGs.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: This could be an impossible question but as we wrap up here, you are at a cocktail party and you mention this course you teach and someone asks you well what makes black music black music?

Well that is a good question. But Duke Ellington had a great answer. He said, “Great music is great music, no matter what. I don’t care if it’s country, jazz, pop, big band. Great music is great music.” And that’s really the way it is. And I know, I think, in my prime I could play black music as good as anybody. And I certainly worked — the guys in Muscle Shoals, that was an all-white rhythm section that played on all those massive Aretha hits. That sounded as black as anything could sound. So I don’t think it’s the color of your skin, it’s like Booker T and the MGs in Memphis — two white guys and two black guys. And they played on Otis Redding, Sam & Dave, Rufus and Carla Thomas, all

those great records. It was an integrated rhythm section. But that was a segregated — Memphis was certainly a segregated city in the 60s. It was rough. But it was Booker T and the MGs. Booker T Jones, black, on keyboards; Al Jackson on drums, black; Steve Cropper, white, on guitar; and Duck Dunn, white, on bass. But that was as black as a — I mean that was really deep funk soul music.
